# Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them

###### Abstract

Experience-driven self-evolution offers a promising path for large
language model (LLM) agents to continually improve through interaction.
Yet existing approaches often rely on successful trajectories or
external evaluation signals, leaving unclear whether agents can evolve
when such positive anchors are unavailable. We study this question
through _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_ (CFOE), where agents start
without accumulated experience and learn only from failed interactions
without privileged guidance. Across three self-evolving paradigms,
multiple LLM backbones, and four interactive environments, we uncover a
consistent _repair–generalization gap_: failure-derived experience can
help repair previously failed tasks, but rarely yields sustained
improvements on unseen tasks. Further analysis shows that agents often
misinterpret failures, while even verified-correct experience remains
difficult to transfer. Relaxing CFOE reveals that verifier feedback and
additional interaction provide limited gains, whereas successful
trajectories substantially improve transfer. These findings suggest that
current self-evolving agents are better at repairing observed failures
than building generalizable capabilities from failure.

## 1 Introduction

With the arrival of the era of experience, large language model (LLM)
agents are increasingly expected to improve through their own
interactions ([Silver and Sutton, 2025](#bib.bib23)). Self-evolving
agents have therefore emerged as a promising paradigm that continually
accumulates and reuses interaction experience ([Dou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Cai et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Bell et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27); [Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)).

![Refer to caption]()

Figure 1: _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_ on a backbone-specific,
failure-dense online task stream. Starting from an empty external state,
agents learn only from failed interactions, without access to
ground-truth answers, expert solutions, or verifier feedback. We
investigate whether existing self-evolving agents can turn
failure-derived experience into transferable capability under these
conditions.

Yet existing self-evolution studies typically assume access to positive
learning signals, such as successful trajectories, verifier feedback, or
already useful experience ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [Yang et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib38); [Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib6)). In
challenging open environments, however, these signals may be scarce
precisely when adaptation is most needed: agents can start without prior
experience, repeatedly fail on unfamiliar tasks, and receive little
guidance on how to improve. This regime provides a critical test of
autonomous self-evolution—whether agents can bootstrap new capabilities
from failure itself, rather than relying on success as a prerequisite
for learning.

To study this problem, we introduce _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_
(CFOE), a setting that isolates self-evolution from failures themselves
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
Agents start from an empty external state and evolve over a
failure-dense online task stream. Successful executions may occur, but
they are used only for evaluation and never for reflection or updating.
Verifier feedback, reward scores, ground-truth answers, and expert
solutions are also hidden from the agent and updater. Thus,
self-evolution is driven exclusively by failed interactions, requiring
agents to diagnose failures and extract reusable experience without
privileged guidance.

We first investigate (RQ1) to what extent agents can learn from failures
under Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution, and whether such learning
generalizes to unseen tasks
(§[3](#S3 "3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
We evaluate three representative paradigms—ReasoningBank for
reasoning-memory evolution ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), SkillOpt
for skill evolution ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib6)), and Evo-Harness
for runtime harness evolution ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib7))—across
multiple LLM families and four interactive environments. Across
frameworks, models, and environments, we observe a consistent
_repair–generalization gap_: failure-derived experience can partially
recover previously failed tasks, yet these gains rarely translate into
sustained improvements on unseen tasks and may even degrade held-out
performance. Extending evolution to much longer horizons does not close
this gap.

We then investigate (RQ2) what prevents failure-derived experience from
becoming transferable capability
(§[4](#S4 "4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
By tracing trajectory interpretation, failure attribution, and
experience consolidation, we identify recurring errors such as
false-success attribution, misattribution, distorted consolidation, and
harmful guidance. These results reveal a diagnosis bottleneck: agents
may turn plausible but unsupported interpretations of failures into
persistent experience. Yet diagnosis alone is not the whole problem.
Even after retaining only verified-correct experience, source-task
recovery improves while held-out performance remains unchanged, showing
that correct experience can still remain overly tied to the source
trajectory and fail to transfer.

Finally, we turn to (RQ3) what learning conditions are missing for
effective experience transfer
(§[5](#S5 "5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
We relax CFOE by allowing successful trajectories, exposing verifier
feedback, or permitting additional interaction during reflection.
Verifier feedback and extra interaction both improve failure
understanding, but yield limited transfer gains. In contrast, successful
interactions produce substantially stronger held-out improvements,
suggesting that positive behavioral evidence provides information that
failure analysis alone cannot easily recover. Failures reveal what went
wrong, while successful trajectories show what reliably works and how
useful actions compose into complete procedures.

Overall, our study provides a controlled evaluation of self-evolution
before success. We show that current agents can extract useful local
corrections from failed interactions, but struggle to turn them into
transferable capability
(§[3](#S3 "3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
We further trace this limitation to unreliable failure interpretation
and the limited transferability of even correct experience
(§[4](#S4 "4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")),
and show that successful behavioral evidence provides substantially
stronger support for transferable evolution than richer failure
diagnosis alone
(§[5](#S5 "5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
These findings suggest that current self-evolving agents are better at
_repairing observed failures_ than at _building generalizable
capabilities from failure_, highlighting a fundamental challenge for
autonomous learning in open environments.

## 2 Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution

We formulate an online self-evolving agent by a fixed backbone policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$, an evolving external state $`S_{t}`$, an updater
$`U`$, and a verifier $`V`$. Given a sequential task stream
$`\{x_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}`$, the agent executes each task with its current
external state,

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \tau_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},S_{t-1}),
       ```                                                 |     |

where $`\theta`$ remains fixed throughout evolution. The updater then
modifies $`S_{t}`$ based on the interaction trajectory. Existing
self-evolving agents mainly differ in the representation of
$`S_{t}`$—e.g., reasoning memory, agent skills, or runtime harness
state—and in how $`U`$ updates it.

Our _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_ (CFOE) setting imposes three
constraints. Evolution starts from an empty external state, only failed
trajectories are used for updating, and all verifier feedback is hidden
from both the agent and the updater. Let
$`y_{t}=V(x_{t},\tau_{t})\in\{0,1\}`$ denote the verifier judgment
available only to the experimental controller. Then

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       S_{t}=\begin{cases}S_{t-1},&y_{t}=1,\\
       U(S_{t-1},\tau_{t}),&y_{t}=0.\end{cases}
       ```                                       |     |

Thus, successful executions may occur occasionally but never contribute
to evolution, while success/failure labels, reward scores, verifier
explanations, ground-truth answers, and expert solutions remain
inaccessible throughout the process.

## 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize

We begin by empirically answering RQ1: to what extent can agents learn
from failures, and whether such learning generalizes to unseen tasks.

### 3.1 Experimental Setup

#### Self-Evolving Agents

We study three paradigms with frozen backbones: reasoning-memory
evolution with ReasoningBank ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), skill
evolution with SkillOpt ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib6)), and runtime
harness evolution with Evo-Harness ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). In
all three frameworks, self-evolution arises from the accumulation and
refinement of external artifacts. Framework details are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Self-Evolving Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

#### Backbone Model.

We conducted experiments with 10 LLM backbones that span multiple model
families, parameter scales, and architectures. Across all three
self-evolution frameworks, we include a wide spectrum of dense variants
of Qwen3.5 family (4B, 9B, and 27B) ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib15)) and
Gemma 4 family (Gemma-4-12B-it and Gemma-4-31B-it) ([Gemma Team,
2026](#bib.bib16)), as well as the mixture-of-experts models
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. We further extend the evaluation
to DeepSeek-V4-Pro ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026](#bib.bib18)), GLM-5.1
([GLM-5-Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)) and GPT-5.6 Sol ([OpenAI,
2026a](#bib.bib21)) in selected frameworks, given the cost of the
held-out evaluation at multiple evolution checkpoints.

#### Environment & Benchmark.

Our experiments cover household embodied task execution, long-horizon
interactive tool use, online shopping, and web navigation across four
_quality-verified_ environments: ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al.,
2021](#bib.bib1)), $`\bm{\tau}^{2}`$-Bench-Verified ([Barres et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20); [Cuadron et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)), WebArena-Verified
([El Hattami et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) (Shopping, Shopping Admin,
Reddit, and GitLab), and WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib4)). These
environments require multi-step interaction and provide a diverse
testbed for long-horizon agentic adaptation. Benchmark details can be
found in the Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Environments and Benchmarks ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

#### Implementation Details.

Closed-source and large-scale open-weight backbones are accessed via
official APIs, while other open-weight models are deployed locally with
vLLM ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)) on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. We adopt the
recommended configurations and evaluation protocols for each agent
framework and benchmark. For SkillOpt, we adapt the offline setup to an
online setting to align with our self-evolution protocol. Further
configurations are provided in the
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Execution Details ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

#### Failure-Dense Online Evolution Streams Construction.

Given the inherent differences in initial task-solving capabilities
across model backbones, we first construct a challenging task stream for
each backbone on each benchmark independently for online self-evolution.
Each task involved in the constructed stream has resulted in a
consistent failure in 3 independent preliminary rollouts with the
corresponding backbone, inducing a high density of failures during
subsequent online self-evolution. Details of the stream construction
procedure are provided in the
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Failure-Dense Online Evolution Streams Construction. ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

#### Online Evolution from Failures Alone

Each run starts with no accumulated memory or skills and a fresh harness
state. The agent processes the challenging task stream sequentially,
using failed trajectories to reflect and evolve its memory, agent
skills, or runtime harness state. Occasional successes are recorded only
for final reporting; the agent moves directly to the next task without
using them for reflection or self-evolution updates.

#### Ground Truth & Reward Blind

The controller uses verifier judgments to collect failed trajectories,
but neither the agent nor updater receives outcome labels, rewards,
verifier explanations, ground-truth answers, or expert solutions. Agents
are also unaware of this failure-only selection. Details of feedback
setting appear in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Verifier Feedback Blind ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

### 3.2 Results and Analysis

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Ground Truth & Reward Blind ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
presents CFOE on ALFWorld and $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified across the
three frameworks. Each benchmark pairs held-out curves with source-task
recovery bars for the same backbones. Results on WebArena-Verified and
WebShop are provided in
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Results Across Models and Benchmarks ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

#### Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution yields limited held-out gains and can even degrade performance.

We evaluate successive checkpoints on a fixed unseen held-out set
disjoint from the online stream. Agent artifacts remain unchanged
throughout evaluation, with no further self-evolution on held-out tasks
(Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Held-Out Evaluation ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
The held-out curves in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Ground Truth & Reward Blind ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
show limited held-out gains, with some configurations even declining as
experience accumulates. SkillOpt exhibits smaller held-out fluctuations
than ReasoningBank and Evo-Harness. This relative stability may stem
from its validation-based acceptance mechanism, which retains candidate
skills only when they improve validation performance. Even so, gains on
held-out tasks remain limited.

#### Failure-derived experience supports partial recovery of original failed tasks.

After each effective update, we retry its failed source tasks once from
their initial states, using the experience state immediately after that
update without further reflection or updates. For these two benchmarks,
recovery is the percentage of successful retries over the entire online
run
(Appendix [C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Source-Task Recovery Evaluation ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
The recovery bars in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Ground Truth & Reward Blind ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
show partial source-task recovery, with rates varying across backbones,
frameworks, and environments. Qwen3.5-27B with SkillOpt recovers more
ALFWorld source tasks than Qwen3.5-4B, yet its held-out performance
still declines. These results show that improvements in source-task
recovery do not reliably carry over to held-out tasks.

### 3.3 Long-Horizon Online Self-Evolution

To examine whether these limitations persist as online self-evolution
scales to a longer horizon, we extend the ALFWorld task stream to 800
episodes. All 800 tasks have failed in three independent preliminary
rollouts with the corresponding backbone and no accumulated experience.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Ground Truth & Reward Blind ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
pairs held-out curves and recovery performance for Qwen3.5-4B,
Qwen3.5-27B, and GLM-5.1 across all three frameworks.

The limited held-out gains persist over the scaled evolution horizon.
Held-out performance declines further for Qwen3.5-27B with Evo-Harness
and plateaus for Qwen3.5-4B with SkillOpt, despite partial source-task
recovery in both configurations. These long-horizon results are
consistent with our earlier observations: failure-derived experience
supports partial source-task recovery, but continued accumulation does
not yield sustained held-out improvements.

## 4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer

To answer RQ2—what prevents agents from turning failure-derived
experience into transferable capability—we conduct two complementary
analyses. We first examine the _faithfulness of experience formation_,
tracing how failed trajectories are interpreted, attributed, and
consolidated into reusable experience
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Errors in Experience Formation ‣ 4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
We then ask whether, even when the extracted experience is correct,
agents can effectively utilize and transfer it to new tasks
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Utilization and Transfer of Correct Experience ‣ 4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).

|                             |          |      |      |      |      |
| --------------------------- | -------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| Model                       | Paradigm | M1   | M2   | M3   | M4   |
| ALFWorld                    |          |      |      |      |      |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Memory   | 41.3 | 46.5 | 32.6 | 35.5 |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Skill    | 43.8 | 39.7 | 28.8 | 37.0 |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Harness  | 29.9 | 38.6 | 31.5 | 36.2 |
| GPT-5.6-Sol                 | Harness  | 21.2 | 31.0 | 25.7 | 23.9 |
| $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified |          |      |      |      |      |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Memory   | 34.0 | 53.2 | 29.8 | 42.6 |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Skill    | 37.8 | 48.6 | 35.1 | 43.2 |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Harness  | 27.9 | 44.2 | 34.9 | 32.6 |
| GPT-5.6-Sol                 | Harness  | 31.7 | 39.0 | 19.5 | 26.8 |
| WebShop                     |          |      |      |      |      |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Skill    | 43.3 | 31.3 | 23.9 | 38.8 |
| Qwen3.5-27B                 | Harness  | 28.2 | 32.4 | 23.9 | 36.6 |
| GPT-5.6-Sol                 | Harness  | 19.7 | 24.6 | 26.2 | 23.0 |

Table 1: Percentage of reviewed updates exhibiting each failure mode. A
single update may exhibit multiple failure modes.

### 4.1 Errors in Experience Formation

To identify the causes of limited experience transfer, we manually
inspect experience accumulated during self-evolution. For each evolution
update, we trace how the agent interprets the failed trajectory, how
this interpretation informs failure attribution, and how the resulting
explanation is consolidated into experience. We analyze Qwen3.5-27B with
ReasoningBank (Memory), SkillOpt (Skill), and Evo-Harness (Harness), and
GPT-5.6-Sol with Evo-Harness. ReasoningBank is evaluated on ALFWorld and
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified; SkillOpt and Evo-Harness are evaluated on
ALFWorld, $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, and WebShop.

We categorize reasons for incorrect experience formation into four
types: (M1) False-Positive Success Attribution (False Success), where
actions or intermediate states that contributed to failure are credited
as successful practices (e.g., treating a budget-wasting exhaustive
search as a successful search strategy). (M2) Misidentified &
Hallucinated Failure Attribution (Misattribution), where relevant causes
are overlooked or replaced with unrelated factors or unsupported
explanations (e.g., falsely interpreting filters on the wrong category
page as evidence that the requested category has been reached). (M3)
Distorted Experience Consolidation (Distortion), where observations or
inferences lose their conditions or acquire unwarranted certainty when
converted into experience (e.g., turning “go back before a new search”
into “always go back from a results page”). (M4) Poisonous Future
Behavior Guidance (Harmful Guidance), where incorrect or unsupported
judgments become direct instructions that badly conflict with
environmental constraints and can lead to further failures (e.g.,
advising agents to abandon troubleshooting and escalate after three
unsuccessful explanations, even when repairs remain available). Some
instances may exhibit more than one failure mode. Detailed annotation
criteria and cases are provided in
Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Annotation Protocol for Experience-Formation Case Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
summarizes the distribution of these errors across models and
benchmarks. Misattribution is particularly common in $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench
Verified, whereas False Success is more prominent in ALFWorld. Stronger
models generally exhibit fewer errors, and harness evolution shows lower
error rates than memory or skill evolution. These error patterns reveal
a weakness in learning under _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_.
Unsupported interpretations of failed attempts may be consolidated into
reusable experience and carried forward as action rules, potentially
guiding subsequent behavior in ways that conflict with task constraints.

![Refer to caption]()

Figure 4: Held-out performance and source-task recovery with full
experience, verified experience, and no experience. Dashed lines denote
the no-experience held-out baseline.

### 4.2 Utilization and Transfer of Correct Experience

#### Setup.

We further investigate whether agents can effectively use
failure-derived experience to improve performance on new tasks, even
when the experience itself is correct. To this end, we retain only
manually verified memory entries or harness modifications at each
checkpoint. We evaluate Qwen3.5-27B with ReasoningBank on ALFWorld and
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, and GPT-5.6-Sol with Evo-Harness on these
benchmarks and WebShop. Full experience, verified experience, and no
experience are compared on the same source and held-out tasks, with
experience fixed during evaluation.

#### Results & Analysis.

Even when the experience extracted from failures is correct, agents
still struggle to apply it effectively to held-out tasks. As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Errors in Experience Formation ‣ 4 Causes of Limited Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them"),
retaining only verified experience modestly improves source-task
recovery in all five configurations, yet final held-out scores remain at
or below the no-experience baseline in four.

These results further indicate the challenge of learning transferable
experience under _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_. Even when the
experience is correct in terms of content, agents still struggle to use
it effectively to form transferable capability. Our inspection shows
that such experience remains tied to specific steps and conditions of
the source task, indicating a gap in extracting generalizable knowledge
from harsh and dense failures.

## 5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer

We next address RQ3: what learning conditions are missing for agents to
acquire more transferable experience? We systematically relax the CFOE
setting along three dimensions by introducing successful experience,
exposing verifier feedback, and allowing additional environment
interaction during failure reflection.

#### Setup.

We adopt the three self-evolving frameworks with Qwen3.5-27B and
evaluate held-out performance on the environments described in
§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
We first vary the source of trajectories available for experience
extraction: (1) Fail: learns only from failed interactions in the
failure-dense task stream, following the original setting in
§[3](#S3 "3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
(2) Success: samples tasks that succeeded in all three preliminary
rollouts and learns only from success during online evolution. (3) Mix:
randomly samples tasks and allows learning from both successful and
failed interactions during online evolution. Task streams are sampled
separately for each setting. We evaluate Success and Mix only with
ReasoningBank and SkillOpt, as Evo-Harness retains its failure-focused
update procedure. In these comparisons, official verifier judgments
remain hidden from the agent and updater, which we denote as Blind.

We next isolate the effect of external evaluative signals by exposing
the official verifier feedback under failure-only evolution (Feedback),
including outcome labels, reward scores, and task-specific feedback
available in each environment.

Finally, we examine whether additional interaction can compensate for
missing information in a failed trajectory. Inspired by the agentic
error analysis in Trace2Skill ([Ni et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)), we allow
the agent to resume interaction with the environment during reflection
(Resume) to diagnose the failure and explore possible corrections.
Reflection is still triggered by the original failed rollout, but the
agent may use observations collected during these additional
interactions when extracting experience, including those from a
subsequently successful attempt. Verifier judgments and ground truth
remain hidden. We allocate 10 interaction turns followed by one
tool-free summary turn in the main comparison. Additional settings and
budget comparisons are provided in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

#### Results & Analysis.

Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
reports held-out performance during online self-evolution under
different learning conditions on ALFWorld and
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified.
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
provides additional results on WebArena-Verified and WebShop. It further
compares 5, 10, and 20 additional interaction turns for Resume, and
evaluates verifier feedback under successful and mixed trajectory
streams.

#### Successful interactions support more effective experience transfer.

As shown in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them"),
learning from successful interactions yields larger held-out
improvements than learning exclusively from failures. Mix also benefits
from incorporating successful interactions, although its gains are
generally smaller than those of Success. Successful trajectories provide
examples of action sequences that complete a task, giving agents
concrete references when extracting reusable experience. These results
suggest that access to successful executions is important for learning
transferable experience.

#### Verifier feedback improves failure-only learning, but its benefits remain limited.

Providing official verifier judgments improves held-out performance
relative to Fail + Blind. The gains nevertheless remain limited compared
with those from successful interactions. Feedback supplies additional
evidence about task outcomes and unmet requirements, but agents must
still infer behavioral corrections and express them as reusable
experience. The remaining transfer difficulties suggest that external
judgment only partially addresses the challenges of learning from failed
interactions.

#### Interactive failure diagnosis offers further learning opportunities with limited transfer gains.

Revisiting failed tasks during reflection also improves held-out
performance over the CFOE baseline. Through additional interactions,
agents can investigate uncertain steps and explore possible corrections
before consolidating experience. These opportunities yield some
transferable gains, although the overall improvement remains limited.
Together with the feedback results, this finding suggests that
additional failure evidence can help learning, while extracting
transferable experience remains challenging.

## 6 Related Work

#### Experience-Driven Self-Evolving Agents.

Recent work explores agents that improve with frozen model parameters by
retaining and reusing interaction experience ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)). Experience can be
collected offline or accumulated during deployment. Offline, AutoGuide
extracts context-aware guidelines from prior trajectories ([Fu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13)). Online approaches update environmental rules through
interaction ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)) or maintain evolving
memories of strategies and code for subsequent queries ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib9)). Voyager stores executable skills ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)), while Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable
workflows ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)). Recent frameworks distill
reasoning memories ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), refine skill
instructions ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib6)), and compile harness
guidance ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). ACE organizes accumulated
strategies into structured playbooks through incremental context updates
([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)). We examine memory, skill, and
harness evolution from a shared cold start as agents learn from failures
on initially challenging tasks.

#### Learning from Failure.

Failure learning has been studied through reflection, feedback, and
experience reuse. Reflexion stores reflections on task feedback to guide
subsequent trials ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)), while ExpeL
contrasts failed and successful executions to derive cross-task rules
([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)). Output revision uses model-generated
feedback in Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)) and
tool-based feedback in CRITIC ([Gou et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)). For
persistent experience updates, ReasoningBank builds memories from
self-judged trajectories ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), and ERL
examines failure-derived heuristics and extraction without outcome
feedback ([Allard et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)). Other approaches check
updates against additional evidence. HarnessFix grounds diagnoses in
execution traces and harness artifacts and validates proposed repairs
([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)); Sentry retains recovery lessons after
checking subsequent interactions and evaluates reuse on unseen tasks
without task-level rewards ([Ji et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)). These
studies connect failure diagnosis to subsequent behavior across feedback
conditions. We study failure-dense learning from unsuccessful
interactions without verifier explanations, separately evaluating
source-task repair and held-out transfer.

## 7 Conclusion

We study whether self-evolving LLM agents can acquire transferable
capability from failure alone through _Cold-Start Failure-Only
Evolution_ (CFOE). Across multiple self-evolving paradigms, LLM
backbones, and interactive environments, we uncover a consistent
_repair–generalization gap_: failure-derived experience can repair
observed failures but rarely transfers to unseen tasks. Further analyses
show that both unreliable failure interpretation and limited transfer of
even correct experience contribute to this gap. Successful trajectories
provide substantially stronger transfer gains than verifier feedback or
additional failure exploration, suggesting that current agents are
better at learning _what went wrong_ than _what reliably works_.

## Limitations

While our study provides a systematic investigation into the limitations
of cold-start failure-only evolution in LLM agents, several limitations
remain. First, our evaluation prioritizes challenging tasks from a
focused set of benchmarks that span both web-based and embodied
scenarios. However, these benchmarks may not fully capture the diversity
of difficult situations agents encounter in real-world deployment
environments, especially those involving multi-agent interactions or
multi-modal inputs. Extending our analysis to broader distributions of
challenging tasks remains an important direction. Second, our
experiments study only scale self-evolving agents over a finite number
of self-evolution steps, with the longest evaluation covering 800 tasks
on ALFWorld. While this already reveals persistent limitations in
experience transfer, real-world deployed agents may undergo
self-evolution over far longer, and potentially unbounded, time
horizons. How experience transfer evolves under such indefinite failure
accumulation, and whether transferable gains emerge beyond the studied
regime, remain open questions for future work and more scaling
exploration.

Overall, this work provides an empirical investigation into the limits
of learning from failures in self-evolving agents. We hope future
efforts will explore more general, principled, and verifiable mechanisms
to support transferable learning from failures in experience-driven AI
systems.

## Ethical Considerations

This work is conducted solely for research purposes, with the goal of
understanding the limitations of learning from failures in self-evolving
agents. All experiments are performed in controlled benchmark
environments, with restricted learning signals used to study experience
formation and transfer. We believe that systematically identifying and
characterizing errors in accumulated experience is important for
reducing the risk of repeated mistakes that could affect users in
real-world applications. By exposing failure modes and transfer
limitations in current self-evolving frameworks, this work aims to
inform the design of evaluation and oversight mechanisms for more
reliable and responsible agentic systems.

## Appendix A Self-Evolving Agents

We present detailed overviews of the three self-evolving agent
frameworks used in our experiments: ReasoningBank, SkillOpt, and
Evo-Harness. These frameworks represent three distinct self-evolution
paradigms, evolving a reasoning memory repository, agent skills, and
runtime harness, respectively, while keeping the underlying model
weights fixed. We introduce the core design and update mechanism of each
framework below.

- •
  ReasoningBank exemplifies a memory-evolution paradigm for reasoning
  memory consolidation. It maintains a continuously growing memory that
  stores distilled reasoning patterns extracted from the agent’s own
  interaction history, including both successful and failed attempts.
  After each task execution, ReasoningBank reflects on the interaction
  trajectory and distills the experience into higher-level memory items
  intended for reuse across tasks. For each new task, relevant memory
  items are retrieved and incorporated into the model context to guide
  subsequent reasoning and actions. Under _Cold-Start Failure-Only
  Evolution_, all trajectories admitted to evolution are harsh failures.
  ReasoningBank therefore has to extract experience exclusively from
  failed interactions, with no end-to-end successful trajectories that
  directly demonstrate effective workflows or provide success–failure
  comparison.
- •
  SkillOpt adopts a skill-evolution paradigm in which a natural-language
  skill document serves as the trainable external artifact for a frozen
  execution agent. During training, SkillOpt iteratively refines its
  skill document across successive rollout batches. After each batch, it
  organizes successful and failed trajectories into separate reflection
  minibatches. The optimizer reflects on these minibatches to propose
  structured edits to the current skill. The proposed edits are then
  aggregated and ranked, with selected edits applied within a fixed
  textual edit budget to produce a candidate skill. SkillOpt then
  evaluates the candidate skill on a held-out validation split, separate
  from the test set, and adopts it only if it outperforms the current
  skill. Rejected edits and their validation outcomes are retained to
  inform subsequent optimization, while slow updates and meta-skill
  memory provide guidance across epochs. Under _Cold-Start Failure-Only
  Evolution_, only harsh failures are accessible, so SkillOpt revises
  its skill using reflection minibatches drawn exclusively from failed
  trajectories.
- •
  Evo-Harness evolves the harness of a frozen base agent through
  context-to-harness skill compilation, converting execution experience
  into reusable guidance. The resulting harness combines general
  strategies applicable across tasks with specialized procedures for
  recurring task types, interfaces, and domains. Before each task,
  Evo-Harness retrieves relevant guidance from the current harness and
  incorporates it into the agent’s context to support planning, tool
  use, verification, and recovery. It then examines failed or negatively
  evaluated trajectories to extract candidate lessons, recording the
  supporting evidence and conditions under which each lesson may apply.
  After each batch, an evolver reviews these lessons against the
  existing harness and decides which to incorporate, merge, or discard.
  Lessons associated with recurring task types, interfaces, or domains
  are integrated into the corresponding topic-specific procedures, while
  patterns shared across tasks are used to update the general
  strategies. The updated harness then guides subsequent tasks, allowing
  both general and topic-specific guidance to evolve as experience
  accumulates. Under _Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution_, we follow this
  evolution process but restrict all experience updates to harsh failure
  trajectories.

## Appendix B Environments and Benchmarks

Our experiments span diverse agentic settings, including household
embodied task execution, long-horizon interactive tool use, online
shopping, and complex web navigation/assistance. All environments
guarantee multi-turn, long-horizon interaction rather than single-shot
decisions; for instance, $`\bm{\tau}^{2}`$-Bench-Verified allows
trajectories of up to 200 steps, highlighting long-horizon planning and
recovery. However, because our method surrounds harsh failures, we pay
extra attention to choose environments whose task instructions and
infrastructure are community verified or otherwise guaranteed to be
solvable (e.g., ALFWorld goals aligned with expert-validated ALFRED
tasks, human-authored WebShop requests, and the verified releases of
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and WebArena). This choice helps ensure that observed
failures are mainly attributable to task difficulty and agent capability
limitations, rather than tasks being inherently unsatisfiable or
requiring unreachable environment states. In the following, we describe
each environment and the data overview used in our study.

### B.1 Household Embodied Environment

ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib1)) provides text-based
household environments aligned with the embodied tasks in ALFRED
([Shridhar et al., 2020](#bib.bib33)). Given a task instruction, the
agent moves to explore the environment, locate objects, and manipulate
them through text commands. Completing these tasks requires the agent to
track the locations and states of the objects and perform actions in the
order required by the task instruction. We use the TextWorld interface
([Côté et al., 2019](#bib.bib34)) and combine the 3,553 training tasks
with the 140 seen-validation tasks to form a candidate pool of 3,693
tasks. All 134 unseen-validation tasks are reserved for held-out
evaluation.

### B.2 Long-horizon Interactive Tool Use

$`\bm{\tau}^{2}`$-Bench-Verified ([Barres et al., 2026](#bib.bib20);
[Cuadron et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) is an interactive tool-use benchmark
that spans the airlines, retail, and telecom domains. Agents gather
information through multi-turn dialog with a simulated user, reason over
domain policies, and execute tool calls to complete requests. These
calls allow the agent to inspect records and modify the environment
state, with later actions depending on information and results obtained
earlier in the interaction. The verified release corrects
inconsistencies among task instructions, expected actions, policies, and
database contents in the original benchmark. In our experiments, we use
GPT-5.5 ([OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib22)) as the default user simulator. Our
candidate pool comprises 178 training tasks across the three domains,
and the 100 test tasks form the holdout set. We use the benchmark’s
official evaluator and count a task as successful only when it receives
the full reward of 1 and ends with a valid conversation termination.

### B.3 Web Environment

#### WebArena-Verified

([El Hattami et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) provides a curated set of tasks
on functional websites, with deterministic evaluators that check agent
responses and recorded browser network activity. We use version 1.2.3
and evaluate four sites separately: Shopping, Shopping Admin, Reddit,
and GitLab. These sites cover online shopping, shopping administration,
social forum, and collaborative software development. Agents follow
natural-language instructions by navigating pages, finding information,
and performing requested operations through the browser. Within each
site, we sampled approximately one quarter of the tasks across templates
for held-out evaluation and use the remaining tasks as candidates for
evolution-stream construction. The set of held-outs contains 47
Shopping, 46 Shopping Admin, 27 Reddit, and 45 GitLab tasks; their
corresponding candidate pools contain 140, 136, 79, and 135 tasks. A
task is successful when all checks required by the official
verified-version evaluator pass.

#### WebShop

([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib4)) is a simulated e-commerce environment
with a catalog of 1.18 million real-world products and 12,087
human-written shopping instructions. Each task requires an agent to find
and purchase an item that satisfies the requested attributes, options,
and budget. The agent must interpret the request, formulate search
queries, and extract relevant information from product pages to guide
its choices. Our experiments use a fixed set of 500 tasks that span
beauty, electronics, fashion, gardening, and grocery products. We
reserve 80 tasks through category-stratified sampling for held-out
evaluation and treat the remaining 420 as the candidate pool for
evolution. Evaluation reports the mean task reward on a 0–1 scale. A
reward of 1 denotes full matches.

## Appendix C Implementation Details

### C.1 Execution Details

We provide additional implementation details for maximum step budgets
set by each environment and how we adapt SkillOpt from its original
offline paradigm to online self-evolution setting in this work. All
frameworks use the same underlying model for both rollout and
reflection.

#### Rollout settings.

We allow up to 30 rollout steps for ALFWorld and WebArena-Verified, 200
steps for $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, and 20 steps for WebShop. The
allocated step budgets provide sufficient chance for agents to complete
the corresponding tasks. The four benchmarks have also been rigorously
reviewed by previous researchers. ALFWorld provides expert trajectories
demonstrating that its tasks are solvable, while WebShop uses
human-written shopping instructions that have been manually reviewed.
For $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and WebArena, we adopt their verified releases to
support more reliable and consistent evaluation.

#### SkillOpt Adaptation.

We adapt SkillOpt from the official _offline_ paradigm to an _online_
self-evolution setting. The online task stream can be traversed once
rather than for multiple epochs. After each batch of task executions,
SkillOpt organizes trajectories into reflection minibatches and proposes
suggestive skill edits. The candidate skill is then evaluated using
SkillOpt’s original validation gate, while the held-out set is reserved
exclusively for checkpoint evaluation. Under the blind setting,
validation scores are used only by the controller to accept or reject
candidate skills; neither the execution nor the reflection agent
receives these scores or verifier feedback. Blindness thus concerns the
information available to these agents, with score-based selection
retained at the controller level.

### C.2 Failure-Dense Online Evolution Streams Construction.

For each benchmark, we construct a backbone-specific online task stream
by selecting tasks that consistently challenge the backbone from the
candidate pool described in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Environments and Benchmarks ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
We run a baseline react agent ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib32)) (without
external experience) on each candidate task up to three independent
attempts, and keep tasks that fail all runs, with infrastructure and
evaluator errors strictly excluded. This process filters out tasks that
can be luckily solved by chance on a retry and leaves tasks that are
consistently difficult for the base agent. We then sample without
replacement to balance the final stream across task type (ALFWorld),
domain ($`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified), and product category (WebShop).
For WebArena-Verified, we construct a separate stream for each site. We
target 200 tasks for ALFWorld, 50 for $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, 80
for WebShop, and 30 per WebArena-Verified site. If fewer tasks qualify 3
failures, we include all of them as failure-dense online evolution
stream.

### C.3 Verifier Feedback Blind

Table [2](#A3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ C.3 Verifier Feedback Blind ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
presents representative examples of the verifier feedback withheld under
the blind setting described in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
These examples include outcome labels, reward scores, and detailed
checks of task completion. The agent retains access to interaction
observations, including action outcomes, state changes, and execution
errors, which provide the local evidence for experience extraction.

### C.4 Held-Out Evaluation

For each benchmark, we reserve a fixed held-out set before constructing
the online evolution stream, as described in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Environments and Benchmarks ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
The agent is evaluated on the same tasks at successive checkpoints,
including the initial state and the final checkpoint. Each task is
executed once from its initial state under the benchmark’s execution
budget. The checkpoint’s complete memory, skill, or harness remains
fixed across all held-out tasks. Reflection and experience updates are
disabled, and held-out trajectories and evaluation feedback are not used
in subsequent online updates. For SkillOpt, the held-out set is separate
from the validation set used to accept or reject candidate skills.

Performance is measured by task success rate on ALFWorld,
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, and WebArena-Verified, and by mean official
score on WebShop. Each checkpoint contributes one point to its
configuration’s held-out curve; the curve includes both the initial
state and the final checkpoint.

### C.5 Source-Task Recovery Evaluation

The original online execution establishes that each source task failed
before its trajectory was used for an update. For each effective update,
we freeze the complete experience state immediately after the update and
give every valid source task one further attempt from its initial state,
using the original execution budget. ReasoningBank is evaluated after
each memory update, with source-task memories eligible for its native
retrieval. SkillOpt includes only accepted proposals, and Evo-Harness
includes only batches that change the harness content. Reflection,
experience updates, and validation are disabled during recovery
evaluation, and recovery results are not returned to the updater.

Each configuration produces a single recovery score by aggregating these
attempts over the entire online run. For ALFWorld,
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, and WebArena-Verified, this is the total
number of successful recovery attempts divided by the total number of
valid recovery attempts. For WebShop, we average official scores over
those attempts. Each valid recovery attempt contributes equally to the
aggregate. The evaluated source sets depend on each framework’s online
trajectories and update decisions. Invalid or incomplete evaluations are
reported separately and are not counted as task failures or zero scores.

## Appendix D Additional Experimental Results

![Refer to caption]()

Figure 6: Held-out performance and source-task recovery during
cold-start failure-only evolution on WebArena-Verified (ReasoningBank)
and WebShop (SkillOpt and Evo-Harness). WebArena-Verified reports task
success rates; WebShop reports mean official scores. N/A indicates that
no SkillOpt candidate update passed validation, leaving no accepted
updates for recovery evaluation.

### D.1 Results Across Models and Benchmarks

Figure [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
presents ReasoningBank results on the four WebArena-Verified sites and
WebShop results for SkillOpt and Evo-Harness, with eight backbones in
each panel. As in the main figures, each configuration is represented by
a held-out curve and a recovery bar. WebArena-Verified reports task
success rates; WebShop reports mean official scores for both held-out
evaluation and recovery. Recovery bars aggregate attempts over the
entire online run.

#### WebArena-Verified: Limited transfer across sites.

Across the four sites, most configurations finish at or below their
initial held-out TSR. For example, Qwen3.5-4B declines from 25.93% to
7.41% on Reddit, while DeepSeek-V4-Pro remains at 47.83% on Shopping
Admin. Recovery rates range from 3.5% to 15.4%, indicating that some
original failures can be recovered even when held-out performance does
not improve. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, recovers 11.1% of source
tasks on Reddit, while its held-out TSR falls from 55.56% to 48.15%.
These results extend the main finding to web navigation: partial
recovery of source tasks does not consistently translate into
improvements on new tasks.

#### WebShop: Held-out gains remain limited across configurations.

Most configurations show little change or lower held-out scores after
self-evolution. GPT-5.6-Sol with Evo-Harness declines from 31.06% to
23.79%, while GLM-5.1 with SkillOpt changes only from 27.40% to 27.70%.
Some SkillOpt configurations improve, including Qwen3.5-27B from 21.64%
to 32.18%, but these gains do not extend across the evaluated backbones
and frameworks. Recovery scores range from 2.5% to 11.8% among
configurations with valid recovery evaluations. Together, the held-out
and recovery results indicate limited benefits from _Cold-Start
Failure-Only Evolution_ in online shopping, with gains concentrated in a
subset of configurations.

### D.2 Annotation Protocol for Experience-Formation Case Study

#### Annotators.

We hired three annotators to conduct the manual inspection and labeling.
All annotators are young adults with higher-education backgrounds (i.e.,
currently enrolled in or graduated from a university program). They were
financially compensated following a pre-agreed hourly rate.

#### Annotation scope and unit.

We focus on experience updates produced during CFOE. Each annotation
instance consists of: (i) the original task and context, (ii) the failed
trajectory or trajectories used for the update, (iii) the corresponding
reflection, and (iv) the resulting memory entry, skill edit, or harness
modification, with the relevant content before and after an edit.
Annotators record each failure mode supported by the evidence, allowing
multiple modes to co-occur in the same instance.

#### Label set and detailed criteria.

We categorize reasons for incorrect experience formation into the
following four types:

- •
  False-Positive Success Attribution, where actions, procedures, or
  intermediate states that contributed to failure are credited as
  effective steps and retained as successful practices (e.g., an
  exhaustive search that consumes the interaction budget is recorded as
  a successful search strategy). Detailed examples are shown in
  Table [3](#A4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ D.4 Experience-Formation Cases ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
- •
  Misidentified & Hallucinated Failure Attribution, where the reflection
  overlooks relevant failure causes, attributes failure to unrelated
  factors, or introduces explanations unsupported by the trajectory and
  environment (e.g., falsely treating filters on the wrong category page
  as confirmation that the requested category has been reached, leaving
  the actual category mismatch undiagnosed). Detailed examples are shown
  in
  Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.4 Experience-Formation Cases ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
- •
  Distorted Experience Consolidation, where observations or inferences
  lose necessary conditions, acquire broader applicability, or become
  more certain when converted into reusable experience (e.g., the
  requirement to go back before issuing a new search becomes a rule to
  always go back from a results page). Detailed examples are shown in
  Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.4 Experience-Formation Cases ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
- •
  Poisonous Future Behavior Guidance, where incorrect or unsupported
  judgments are converted into actionable rules that can induce further
  failures when reused (e.g., instructing agents to stop troubleshooting
  and escalate after three unsuccessful explanations, even when
  executable repairs remain; subsequent agents follow this rule and
  leave those repairs unattempted). Detailed examples are shown in
  Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.4 Experience-Formation Cases ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").

### D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions

We provide the settings and additional comparisons for
§[5](#S5 "5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
All conditions use Qwen3.5-27B. The failure-only comparison covers 12
framework–benchmark configurations: all three frameworks on ALFWorld and
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench-Verified, ReasoningBank on four WebArena-Verified
sites, and SkillOpt and Evo-Harness on WebShop. Success and Mix cover
the nine ReasoningBank and SkillOpt configurations.

#### Learning material and feedback.

Fail + Blind reuses the CFOE results reported in
Figures [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Ground Truth & Reward Blind ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Failure-Only Evolution Repairs but Does Not Generalize ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
and [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
Success selects tasks that succeeded in all three preliminary rollouts
and admits only successful online interactions to learning. Mix uses
randomly sampled tasks and admits both outcomes, without imposing a
fixed success-to-failure ratio. Feedback exposes the official verifier
judgments illustrated in
Table [2](#A3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ C.3 Verifier Feedback Blind ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them"),
including expected actions and their arguments where available. No
expert trajectories or complete reference solutions are provided.
Figure [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
extends the main comparison to web navigation and online shopping.

#### Interactive diagnosis budget.

We compare 5, 10, and 20 additional interaction turns, each followed by
one tool-free summary turn
(Figure [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")).
The interaction budget applies to diagnosis during reflection and is
separate from the original task-execution budget. The original rollout
remains recorded as a failure regardless of subsequent attempts.
Reflection can use all evidence gathered during diagnosis, while
official verifier judgments and ground truth remain hidden. This
comparison examines whether more opportunities to investigate a failure
yield experience that transfers to unseen tasks.

#### Feedback with successful and mixed interactions.

Figure [9](#A4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
includes only Success + Feedback and Mix + Feedback, with initial
performance as a reference. The corresponding blind conditions appear in
Figures [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
and [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
This comparison examines the usefulness of verifier judgments when
successful executions are already available for learning.

#### Evaluation and interpretation.

We evaluate held-out performance with experience fixed, following
Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Held-Out Evaluation ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them").
These comparisons concern transfer to unseen tasks; successful attempts
during diagnosis are not counted as source-task recovery results.
Different conditions need not share task streams or update schedules.
For SkillOpt, inherited checkpoints retain the accepted skill, and an
accepted update is distinct from an evaluation checkpoint.

#### Successful interactions improve transfer in additional environments.

Figure [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
extends the main comparison to web navigation and online shopping.
Success yields the highest final held-out performance on the four
WebArena-Verified sites and with SkillOpt on WebShop. Mix also improves
over the initial reference, although its final performance remains below
Success. The failure-based conditions show more varied benefits:
Feedback and Resume improve on Fail + Blind in several configurations,
while their final scores overlap with other conditions in some settings.
These results extend the main observation that successful interactions
provide useful material for transferable experience, while additional
judgment or exploration offers more limited benefits when learning
starts from failures.

#### Increasing the diagnosis budget yields limited additional gains.

Figure [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
compares 5, 10, and 20 interaction turns, each followed by one tool-free
summary turn. Allowing interactive diagnosis improves final held-out
performance over Fail + Blind, and larger budgets generally produce
higher final scores. The differences between budgets are modest, with
some configurations reaching the same final score under two budgets. For
example, ReasoningBank on Reddit finishes at the same level with 5 and
10 interaction turns despite differences during learning. Additional
opportunities to investigate a failure therefore help, but the small
gains from extending the budget suggest that more interaction alone only
partially addresses the difficulty of extracting transferable
experience.

#### Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions.

Figure [9](#A4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
reports Success + Feedback and Mix + Feedback, both of which improve
over initial held-out performance. Compared with their blind
counterparts in
Figures [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ 5 Effects of Learning Conditions on Experience Transfer ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them")
and [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Feedback also benefits learning with successful and mixed interactions. ‣ D.3 Effects of Learning Conditions ‣ Appendix D Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them"),
feedback provides additional gains in several configurations,
particularly for Mix. These gains vary across environments; Success, for
example, reaches the same final score with and without feedback on
several WebArena-Verified sites. This comparison suggests that verifier
judgments can complement successful examples, while the benefits depend
on the learning material already available. Together with the
failure-only comparison, the results indicate that the usefulness of
external judgment depends on the interactions from which agents extract
experience.
